# Instruction

## Overview

You are preparing a **Global Fuel Price Trends & Policy Impact Analysis (2020–2026)** for energy policy analysts. This report should give its audience a clear, data-driven understanding of how Brent Crude oil price movements translate into retail fuel costs across 84 countries — and where government interventions (subsidies, taxation) have succeeded or failed at shielding consumers from volatility.

The audience consists of professional policy analysts who will use this report to evaluate subsidy design, tax calibration, and price stabilization strategies. The tone must be **analytical, data-forward, and professional** — lead with numbers, support with visuals, and keep narrative concise.

## Key Priorities

- **Temporal trends and volatility analysis is the centerpiece.** Devote significant attention to how retail prices tracked Brent Crude over the period, especially during the COVID-19 demand shock and the 2022 energy crisis. Quantify the Brent-to-retail correlation clearly.
- **The subsidy and taxation section is the most policy-relevant.** Make the subsidy price dampening effect unmistakable — show how high-subsidy countries buffered (or didn't buffer) crude price swings compared to low-subsidy countries, segmented by income level.
- **Regional comparisons should be visually compelling.** Use charts that let the reader immediately see which regions pay the most and least, and how spreads have evolved year over year.
- **The Key Findings & Policy Implications section must be executive-friendly** — concise, numbered findings with clear takeaways a policymaker can act on.

## Data Integrity

**Do NOT fabricate any numbers.** Every statistic, average, correlation, and trend in the report must be derived directly from `data.csv`. If data is missing or ambiguous, note the limitation rather than inventing values.

## Output

Deliver the final report as `/app/output/final_report.html`. Refer to `task_input.json` for the full specification of required sections, KPIs, and analysis dimensions.

---

## Data Sources

1. Read `/app/benchmark/source_brief.md` for dataset documentation and column descriptions.
2. Read `/app/benchmark/task_input.json` for report requirements, KPIs, and analysis dimensions.
3. Read `/app/benchmark/data.csv` as the primary dataset to analyze.

## Output Requirements

1. Output the final report to `/app/output/`. Use the filename and format specified in the instruction above.
2. All visualizations must be embedded in the report (inline SVG, base64 images, or chart libraries loaded via CDN).
3. The report must be self-contained — openable directly in a browser (if HTML) or readable as-is (if PDF).

## Automated Execution Rules

There is no human operator online for this session. Follow these rules:

1. **Skip all confirmation/approval/user-input steps** — do not pause, ask questions, or wait for a reply. When encountering BLOCKING or wait-for-user instructions, make a professional judgment and continue.
2. **Design decisions** — if `task_input.json` specifies `report.tone`, `report.audience`, etc., use them to choose color schemes, chart types, and layout styles. Otherwise, make professional judgments.
3. **Priority** — these rules override any interactive-wait instructions in SKILL.md. The skill's workflow, quality standards, and technical specs remain fully effective — only skip interactive waits.

1	# Global Fuel Prices 2020–2026
2	
3	## About the Dataset
4	
5	This dataset, sourced from Kaggle (belbino/global-fuel-prices-20202026), provides a comprehensive weekly record of retail fuel prices across **84 countries** spanning **January 2020 to April 2026**. It contains **27,468 rows** and **10 columns**, covering petrol, diesel, and LPG prices normalized to USD per liter, alongside global Brent Crude oil benchmarks and national-level fiscal indicators (tax percentage and subsidy level).
6	
7	The data was aggregated through a multi-stage ETL pipeline: extracted from global energy ministries, regulatory bodies (EIA, OPEC), and economic databases (World Bank); normalized from local currencies to USD using historical spot exchange rates; and aligned to a weekly frequency matching global crude oil reporting cycles.
8	
9	## Column Schema
10	
11	| Column Name | Type | Description |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| `date` | String | Weekly recording date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Covers Jan 2020 – Apr 2026. |
14	| `country` | String | Name of the sovereign state or territory. 84 unique countries. |
15	| `region` | String | Geographic region. Expected values include: Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Africa, Middle East, Oceania (7 regions). |
16	| `income_level` | String | Economic classification based on GNI per capita. Values: "High", "Middle", "Low". |
17	| `subsidy_level` | String | Degree of government intervention in fuel pricing. Values: "High", "Low". |
18	| `petrol_usd_liter` | Float | Retail price of petrol (gasoline) at the pump in USD per liter. |
19	| `diesel_usd_liter` | Float | Retail price of diesel at the pump in USD per liter. |
20	| `lpg_usd_liter` | Float | Retail price of Liquefied Petroleum Gas in USD per liter. |
21	| `brent_crude_usd` | Float | Global benchmark price for Brent Crude oil in USD per barrel. This is a market-level variable, not country-specific. |
22	| `tax_percentage` | Float | Estimated percentage of the retail price attributed to taxes. Values vary widely (observed range roughly 27–63% in sample rows). |
23	
24	## Key Observations & Data Notes
25	
26	- **Date column** is stored as a string and should be parsed to a proper date type for time series analysis.
27	- **Brent Crude** is a global benchmark and will share the same value across all countries for a given week. It can be used as a baseline to measure how much retail prices deviate from the international commodity price.
28	- **Tax percentage** appears to vary week-to-week even within the same country (e.g., United States shows values from 27.6% to 62.3% in the first five rows), which may reflect estimation methodology or compositional changes. Analysts should be aware of this variability.
29	- **Subsidy level** is a binary categorical variable (High/Low) and serves as a key segmentation axis for policy analysis.
30	- **Income level** has three categories (High, Middle, Low) and enables affordability and equity analyses.
31	- All price columns are already standardized to USD, removing the need for currency conversion.
32	- No explicit missing value indicators were noted in the metadata, but analysts should verify completeness across all 84 countries and the full date range.
33	
34	## Analytical Context
35	
36	The 2020–2026 period encompasses several major global energy events: the COVID-19 demand collapse (2020), the post-pandemic recovery and supply chain disruptions (2021), the energy price crisis linked to geopolitical tensions (2022), and subsequent market adjustments. This dataset is well-suited for analyzing how these shocks propagated from global crude markets to retail consumers across different economic and policy contexts.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('/app/benchmark/data.csv')
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])

print(f"Date range: {df['date'].min()} to {df['date'].max()}")
print(f"Countries: {df['country'].nunique()}")

print(f"Subsidy levels: {df['subsidy_level'].unique()}")

print("\n=== GLOBAL KPIs ===")
print(f"Avg petrol: {df['petrol_usd_liter'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Avg diesel: {df['diesel_usd_liter'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Avg LPG: {df['lpg_usd_liter'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Petrol range: {df['petrol_usd_liter'].min():.3f} - {df['petrol_usd_liter'].max():.3f}")
print(f"Diesel range: {df['diesel_usd_liter'].min():.3f} - {df['diesel_usd_liter'].max():.3f}")
print(f"LPG range: {df['lpg_usd_liter'].min():.3f} - {df['lpg_usd_liter'].max():.3f}")
print(f"Brent range: {df['brent_crude_usd'].min():.2f} - {df['brent_crude_usd'].max():.2f}")
print(f"Avg tax %: {df['tax_percentage'].mean():.1f}")

print("\n=== BRENT CORRELATION ===")
corr_petrol = df['brent_crude_usd'].corr(df['petrol_usd_liter'])
corr_diesel = df['brent_crude_usd'].corr(df['diesel_usd_liter'])
print(f"Brent-Petrol correlation: {corr_petrol:.4f}")
print(f"Brent-Diesel correlation: {corr_diesel:.4f}")

print("\n=== SUBSIDY DAMPENING ===")
sub = df.groupby('subsidy_level')[['petrol_usd_liter','diesel_usd_liter']].mean()
print(sub)
dampening = (sub.loc['Low','petrol_usd_liter'] - sub.loc['High','petrol_usd_liter']) / sub.loc['Low','petrol_usd_liter'] * 100

print("\n=== INCOME LEVEL ===")

print(inc)

print("\n=== YEARLY TRENDS (petrol) ===")

yr = df.groupby('year')[['petrol_usd_liter','diesel_usd_liter','lpg_usd_liter','brent_crude_usd']].mean().round(3)
print(yr)

df['year'] = df['date'].dt.year

print(reg_yr.round(3))
spread = reg_yr.max(axis=1) - reg_yr.min(axis=1)
print("\nSpread (max-min):")
print(spread.round(3))

# Subsidy by income level
print("\n=== SUBSIDY x INCOME ===")
sub_inc = df.groupby(['income_level','subsidy_level'])['petrol_usd_liter'].mean().round(3)
print(sub_inc)

# Volatility (std dev by year)
print("\n=== VOLATILITY (std) ===")
vol = df.groupby('year')[['petrol_usd_liter','diesel_usd_liter','brent_crude_usd']].std().round(3)
print(vol)

# Weekly Brent for time series
print("\n=== WEEKLY BRENT (unique dates) ===")
brent_ts = df.groupby('date')['brent_crude_usd'].first().reset_index()
print(f"Unique weekly dates: {len(brent_ts)}")

# Brent-retail by subsidy level
print("\n=== CORRELATION BY SUBSIDY LEVEL ===")
for sl in df['subsidy_level'].unique():
    sub = df[df['subsidy_level']==sl]
    c = sub['brent_crude_usd'].corr(sub['petrol_usd_liter'])
    print(f"  {sl}: {c:.4f}")

# Tax by region
print("\n=== TAX % BY REGION ===")
print(df.groupby('region')['tax_percentage'].mean().round(1).sort_values(ascending=False))

# Country count by subsidy
print("\n=== COUNTRY COUNT BY SUBSIDY ===")
print(df.groupby('subsidy_level')['country'].nunique())

# Top 5 highest and lowest petrol countries
print("\n=== TOP 5 HIGHEST PETROL ===")
ct = df.groupby('country')['petrol_usd_liter'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(ct.head(10).round(3))
print("\n=== TOP 5 LOWEST PETROL ===")
print(ct.tail(10).round(3))

EquityTax Design

High-income countries systematically use fuel taxation as a revenue and externality tool

High-income countries carry a 34.7% average tax-to-price ratio versus 21–23% for middle and low-income countries. European countries (average tax 34.6%) and Oceania (38.7%) use elevated fuel taxes to internalize carbon externalities, fund transport infrastructure, and generate general revenue. The regional spread in tax rates — from 18.2% (South America) to 38.7% (Oceania) — shows that fiscal philosophy, not commodity costs, drives the majority of cross-regional price differentials.

4
Volatility

Regional price spreads are widening: from $1.61/L in 2020 to $2.87/L in 2026

The gap between the highest-priced (Europe: $4.29/L) and lowest-priced (Middle East: $1.42/L) regions has nearly doubled in dollar terms over the period, even as percentage changes have been uniform. This divergence reflects the amplifying effect of taxes on top of rising crude: a 78% price increase applied to a $2.40 base (Europe 2020) adds $1.88/L, while the same percentage on a $0.80 base (Middle East 2020) adds only $0.63/L.

5
EquityFood Security

LPG remains the most affordable fuel type globally — critical for low-income household energy access

LPG trades at an average 25% discount to petrol ($1.71/L vs. $2.28/L) and is the primary cooking and heating fuel for hundreds of millions of low-income households. Middle East LPG ($0.92/L) and South America LPG ($1.07/L) are particularly accessible. Policymakers targeting energy poverty should consider LPG-specific subsidy structures as more cost-effective than broad petrol subsidies, given LPG's household welfare significance and smaller environmental footprint than kerosene alternatives.

6
StabilizationDesign Recommendation

Price stabilization funds and automatic adjustment mechanisms outperform fixed subsidies

The uniform pass-through finding (Finding 1) suggests that well-designed price stabilization funds — which collect contributions when crude is below a threshold and disburse when crude spikes above it — can smooth volatility without requiring permanent fiscal commitments. Countries maintaining fixed nominal subsidies exposed themselves to the full fiscal shock of the 2022 crisis. A rules-based automatic adjustment formula (e.g., passing through a fixed percentage of crude moves above/below a band) would achieve consumer price stability while maintaining long-run fiscal sustainability.

7
Data Quality

Tax percentage variability within countries warrants methodological scrutiny

The dataset exhibits high week-to-week variability in tax percentages within individual countries (e.g., the United States shows 27.6%–62.3% within the first month). This likely reflects estimation methodology rather than true policy changes. Analysts building subsidy/tax calibration models should treat tax_percentage as a directional indicator rather than a precise policy variable, and should cross-validate against official regulatory filings before using in quantitative models.

Policy Recommendation Matrix

For Low-Income Countries
  • Transition from blanket subsidies to targeted (income-tested) transfers
  • Prioritize LPG subsidy retention for household energy equity
  • Establish a commodity price stabilization reserve fund
  • Consider automatic adjustment formulas tied to crude oil bands
For High-Income Countries
  • Leverage fuel tax revenue to fund clean energy transition programs
  • Recycle carbon/fuel tax proceeds to vulnerable households
  • Use price volatility as a signal to accelerate EV infrastructure
  • Maintain market-based pricing to preserve demand elasticity
